ai.definition: Quantum Key Distribution Networks (QKD) are city-scale fiber-optic networks that utilize quantum mechanics to securely distribute encryption keys. These systems ensure secure communication by detecting any eavesdropping attempts, which would alter the quantum state of single photons.
ai.howItWorks: Photons in a quantum state are transmitted between network nodes. Any attempt to intercept these photons will change their quantum state, leading to detectable statistical changes that alert both communicating parties about potential eavesdropping. Trusted relay or twin-field protocols can extend the distance and security of QKD networks.
ai.problemSolved: QKD addresses the fundamental limitations of classical cryptography by providing a method for secure key exchange that is inherently resistant to quantum attacks, thus ensuring confidentiality and integrity in communications over long distances.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing involves creating highly precise optical fibers, single-photon sources, detectors, and control electronics. The process requires specialized equipment and skilled labor, making it complex and costly.
ai.buildProcess: The build process includes designing the network topology, deploying fiber optic cables, integrating quantum devices such as single-photon emitters and detectors, setting up secure communication protocols, and conducting extensive testing to ensure reliability and security.
ai.costDrivers: High costs are driven by the need for advanced quantum optics technology, specialized equipment, skilled labor, and rigorous testing. The complexity of integrating multiple components into a secure network also adds to the expense.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The outlook is promising but faces challenges in scaling and standardization. As research progresses, costs are expected to decrease, making QKD more accessible for broader deployment.
ai.regulation: Regulatory frameworks vary by region, with some governments supporting the development of quantum technologies through funding and policy initiatives. However, specific regulations for QKD networks are still evolving.
ai.risks: Technical risks include the need for continuous error correction, potential vulnerabilities in classical components of the network, and the complexity of ensuring long-term security against emerging quantum computing threats.
ai.profitability: Profitability is currently limited due to high initial costs and narrow target markets. However, as adoption increases and economies of scale are achieved, profitability could improve.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development will focus on improving the efficiency and reliability of QKD systems, reducing costs, and expanding network coverage. Integration with emerging quantum technologies like quantum computers is also anticipated to enhance security capabilities.

glossary.def: A description of the physical properties of a quantum system, such as an electron or photon, that can exist in multiple states simultaneously until measured.
A node in a QKD network designed to securely transmit information between two parties without being able to eavesdrop on the communication.
A method used in QKD networks that combines elements of both prepare-and-measure and measurement-device-independent protocols to enhance security and distance.

subsystems.name: Photon source
subsystems.role: generates the faint laser pulses or single photons that carry the quantum key.

subsystems.name: Quantum channel
subsystems.role: carries photons between nodes without amplification, which would destroy the quantum state.
parts: free-space or satellite link for long distances

subsystems.name: Single-photon detectors
subsystems.role: register individual photons at the receiving node.
parts: superconducting nanowire or avalanche photodiode detectors
cryogenics or cooling for some types

subsystems.name: Classical channel
subsystems.role: authenticated public messages for sifting and error correction.

subsystems.name: Key post-processing
subsystems.role: turns raw detections into a short, secret key.

subsystems.name: Trusted nodes and relays
subsystems.role: extend range by decoding and re-encrypting at intermediate sites.

subsystems.name: Network control
subsystems.role: routes key material and integrates with existing encryption gear.
parts: interface to VPN or optical transport equipment

buildSteps.title: Choose the link and topology
buildSteps.detail: Decide between a dedicated fibre pair, a multiplexed telecom fibre, or a free-space path between buildings.

buildSteps.title: Install quantum endpoints
buildSteps.detail: Place a transmitter at one node and a receiver at the other, with precise optical alignment.

buildSteps.title: Calibrate the optical path
buildSteps.detail: Measure loss and detector dark counts, and tune timing so photons arrive within the detection window.

buildSteps.title: Run the quantum exchange
buildSteps.detail: Send photons in randomly chosen bases; the receiver measures in its own randomly chosen bases and records detections.

buildSteps.title: Sift and correct
buildSteps.detail: Over the authenticated classical channel, the two sides keep matching bases and correct errors without revealing the key.

buildSteps.title: Amplify privacy
buildSteps.detail: Compress the corrected string so that any information an eavesdropper might have is removed, leaving a secret key.

buildSteps.title: Deliver the key
buildSteps.detail: Feed the key into an encryption device — for example, to refresh keys for a VPN or optical link.

buildSteps.title: Extend the network
buildSteps.detail: Add trusted nodes to bridge longer distances, or deploy twin-field QKD to push reach without trusting intermediate sites.

buildSteps.title: Monitor and audit
buildSteps.detail: Continuously check the quantum bit error rate; a rise above the security threshold means the key is discarded and the link investigated.

prerequisites.why: no detector, no quantum key; their efficiency and noise set the maximum distance.
photons cannot be amplified, so every decibel of loss directly shortens the link.
the security proof assumes truly random basis choices and keys.
without it, an attacker could impersonate a node during sifting and error correction.
they would allow entanglement to be extended over long distances without trusted nodes; today's networks rely on trust or short links.
groups such as ETSI have published QKD specifications, but interoperability and security certification are still maturing.

pathway.milestone: metro-scale QKD links and small networks in several countries, plus satellite demonstrations such as Micius (2016)
pathway.unlocks: point-to-point high-assurance key exchange for banks, data centres and government links.

pathway.milestone: integration with telecom networks and hybrid use alongside post-quantum cryptography
pathway.unlocks: QKD where it adds value, with cheaper classical algorithms covering the rest.

pathway.milestone: twin-field QKD and improved detectors extending reach beyond a few hundred kilometres of fibre
pathway.unlocks: regional networks without trusting every intermediate node.
a quantum internet that can also link quantum computers, not just distribute keys.
